Here, we integrate density functional theory (DFT) calculations with plasma-catalytic experiments to investigate direct CH4-to-CH3OH conversion using H2O as the sole oxidant on CuxOy clusters within MOR zeolite, compared to the CuO(111) surface.

title: Measurement-efficient energy estimator for quantum chemistry of photodynamic materials
abstract: Accurate modelling of chemical reaction rates requires precise correlated energy differences. Quantum computing offers a potential route to their determination, but extracting energies from quantum-prepared states can demand prohibitive sampling. We demonstrate measurement-efficient correlated energy estimation using an electronically challenging H$_2$DBB--Ru model derived from a Ru-functionalized hafnium metal-organic framework relevant to radiodynamic and photodynamic therapies. The mixed estimator combines a quantum-prepared target with sparse multiconfiguration references and recovers ground-state corrections using magnitude-only compute-uncompute measurements. Analytical variance estimates predict 1.6 mHa precision with a few hundred shots, about 100 times fewer than the single-determinant formulation and three orders of magnitude fewer than optimized Hamiltonian-term sampling. With approximate targets, it reaches comparable accuracy using simpler state preparation than direct expectation-value estimation. Emulator and trapped-ion experiments on Quantinuum Helios validate the approach up to (10,10), including a 50-qubit circuit combining AI-assisted state preparation with error detection, providing a measurement-efficient route to correlated energy differences for challenging chemical problems.

title: A Probabilistic, Rotation-Preserving Kernel Operator Surrogate for Continuum-Robot Design Spaces
abstract: We develop an uncertainty-aware, operator-learning-based surrogate for tendon-driven continuum robots (TDCRs) that generalizes across robot design and actuation while predicting the complete equilibrium configuration. Our central idea is a nonstationary Gaussian-process (GP) kernel whose metric is learned by a shallow neural network from mechanics-aware design coordinates. The network learns how similarity changes across design space, while the resulting kernel defines the design-to-pose operator, its posterior uncertainty, and a criterion for sequential simulator acquisition. We represent backbone position and rotational strain with spatial kernels and reconstruct orientation directly on SO(3), preserving valid material frames and tendon geometry. We use ASkotch with Nystrom preconditioning for scalable kernel operator solves and a separate Nystrom approximation for posterior covariance. Experiments show that kernel-coverage acquisition reduces mean trajectory error by approximately 15% relative to IID sampling, while posterior variance increases for increasingly unsupported designs. Compared with prior neural-operator TDCR models, the method is 30-50% more accurate using approximately 5x fewer training designs while additionally providing posterior uncertainty estimates.

title: Strain-induced disorder from Schottky gates on high mobility 2DEGs
abstract: Electrostatic gates on two-dimensional electron gases (2DEGs) in GaAs/AlGaAs heterostructures are essential for numerous studies of correlation driven phenomena, many performed within the fractional quantum Hall effect. However, the most commonly used type of gates, the metallic Schottky gate, has the propensity to adversely impact the electron mobility and suppress the fractional quantum Hall states. Here we demonstrate through commensurability oscillations under specially designed nanostructured superlattice gates, that strain effects are responsible for the mobility reduction. The experimental results agree well with COMSOL Multiphysics simulations. In a regular, unpatterned gate the disordered, granular nature of the metal film fills the same role as the superlattice in creating a strain field penetrating down to the 2DEG, as we show with a simplified model. These results will help in understanding, improving and finding novel methods to reduce strain-induced disorder in gated high-mobility 2DEGs.

title: Stabilization of Ferroelectric Domains via Interfacial Strain in HoFeO3- BaTiO3 Nanofiber Heterostructures for Enhanced Hybrid Energy Harvesting
abstract: Piezoelectric nanogenerators (PENGs) are an attractive platform for self-powered mechanical-energy harvesting, but their output is often limited by depolarization fields, charge leakage, and inefficient stress transfer to the active dipoles, particularly in polymer-dominated composites. Here we report HoFeO3-BaTiO3 (HFO-BTO) nanofiber heterostructures prepared by alternating sol-gel electrospinning, in which orthorhombic HoFeO3 (Pbnm) and tetragonal BaTiO3 (P4mm) coexist in intimate contact. Rietveld-refined X-ray diffraction, high-resolution transmission electron microscopy, and Raman spectroscopy indicate interfacial lattice distortion. Polarization-electric field loops show that the heterostructure retains a polarization comparable to that of BaTiO3 (16.39 vs 15.80 microcoulombs per square centimeter at zero field) while its switching-current maximum moves to a higher field (about 7 vs about 3.5 kilovolts per centimeter), consistent with strain-stabilized ferroelectric domains. When the nanofibers are encapsulated in polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) and excited under cyclic impact, the device produces a hybrid output: the piezoelectric response of the strained BaTiO3 is supplemented by a triboelectric contribution from contact electrification. The HFO-BTO device delivers open-circuit voltage peaks of about +6 volts and -8 volts and a power density of 24.31 microwatts per cubic centimeter at a 4.7 megaohm load. This is 2.4 times the value for an identically fabricated BaTiO3 device (10.00 microwatts per cubic centimeter) and 8.7 times that of the HoFeO3 device (2.78 microwatts per cubic centimeter). These results link interface-driven lattice distortion to improved electromechanical output and identify all-oxide nanofiber heterostructures as a promising route to lead-free energy harvesting.

title: The Effectiveness and Durability of Pretraining Data Filtering in Protein Language Models
abstract: Pretraining filtering is one of the most common safeguards for open-weight language models. Here we study its effectiveness, durability and scalability using the ESM-2 family of protein language models. We find that filtering viral proteins from the pretraining data meaningfully degrades masked language modelling, mutation effect prediction and long-range contact prediction on viral proteins, while largely preserving performance on non-viral proteins. These effects are concentrated among proteins from human-infecting viruses, and grow as we scale models from 8M to 3B parameters. As models increase in size, we find that stringent filtering becomes more effective. However, fine-tuning on sequences from the removed viral families restores the lost performance. Although the cost to recover performance increases with model scale, even for the largest models it costs about 80 USD of H100 time. This work establishes pretraining filtering as moderately effective at selectively degrading performance on viral proteins, but not durable against fine-tuning with modest computational resources and access to relevant data.

title: Vacancy and Helium-Cluster Thermomigration in Tungsten
abstract: Strong thermal gradients in tungsten plasma-facing components can bias the migration of irradiation-induced defects and thereby alter their redistribution, interaction, and retention. Here, we extend an atomistic jump-statistics framework previously developed for hydrogen to quantify the thermomigration of a single vacancy and interstitial He$_1$--He$_4$ clusters in body-centered-cubic tungsten. Non-equilibrium molecular-dynamics simulations performed over several thermal gradients are used to determine the directional jump ratio, while geometrically derived projected jump lengths convert the fitted directional-bias coefficient into the heat-of-transport coefficient $Q^*=αkT^2$, where $k$ is the Boltzmann constant, $T$ the temperature, and $α$ a constant. All investigated defects exhibit negative values of $α$, corresponding to net migration toward the hot region. He$_4$ has the largest response, $α=-2.2457\times10^{-2}$ K$^{-1}$, followed closely by the vacancy, whereas He$_3$ exhibits the weakest response despite its intermediate cluster size. Independent constant-temperature simulations over 1000--1600 K show that He$_3$ is also the least mobile cluster and has the largest effective migration energy, $E_m^{\mathrm{eff}}=0.271$ eV. In contrast, He$_4$ is more mobile than He$_3$ and has the smallest effective migration energy, 0.087 eV. Agreement between the He$_3$ concentration profile predicted from the jump statistics and that obtained from a long molecular-dynamics trajectory provides an independent validation of the method. These results show that thermomigration cannot be inferred from cluster size, diffusivity, or migration energy alone and provide defect-specific heat-of-transport parameters for higher-length-scale models of tungsten under fusion-relevant thermal gradients.

title: NIR-probe transient absorption on rubrene microcavities demonstrates no changes to singlet fission by strong coupling
abstract: Strong light-matter coupling has been proposed to control singlet-exciton fission, yet reported effects remain controversial due to the prevalence of cavity-induced optical artifacts in transient absorption measurements. Here, we investigate singlet fission in dielectric microcavities containing rubrene by probing in the near-infrared region, outside the cavity stopband, to eliminate mode-filtering artifacts. Across contrasting cavity quality factors ($Q = 90$ and $1150$) and a range of exciton-photon detunings ($+20$ to $-110$ meV), we find that the underlying kinetics are virtually identical to uncoupled films. Although minor spectral changes occur, transfer matrix simulations reveal these stem purely from mirror interference rather than modified photophysics. Transient electron paramagnetic resonance further confirms that high-spin triplet dynamics remain unperturbed. Together, these findings establish a widely applicable experimental framework for evaluating molecular photophysics in microcavities, revealing that singlet fission remains unaltered in strongly coupled rubrene.

title: Establishing toxicologically relevant primary alveolar macrophage models to enable a realistic assessment of nanomaterials safety
abstract: Alveolar macrophages (AMs) are key sentinels of the distal lung, maintaining surfactant homeostasis and clearing inhaled particles through continuous surveillance and phagocytosis. Mechanistic studies of particle-cell interactions, important to assess the respiratory safety or toxicity of particles, however, are limited by the lack of suitable in vitro models that preserve the core features of resident AMs. Here, we benchmarked six murine AM models, including short-term cultured primary AMs (AMs 3 h, AMs 24 h), primary AMs maintained with GM-CSF, TGF-{beta}, and the PPAR-{gamma} agonist rosiglitazone (AMs GTR), bone marrow-derived AM-like cells (BM-AMs), the immortalized AM cell line MH-S, and the non-transformed fetal liver-derived AM-like cell line MPI, against in vivo AMs based on surface phenotype, transcriptomic identity, and their responses to three carbon-based nanomaterials (CBNs). Both cell lines showed limited AM identity, characterized by low CD11c and SiglecF but high CD11b surface expression. In contrast, AMs GTR and BM-AMs more closely preserved resident AM-like surface marker profiles. Transcriptomic features, although differing for alterations in metabolism-related pathways, particularly oxidative phosphorylation, revealed most in vivo-like for the primary AM models. Functional, toxicological assessment using soot-like carbon nanoparticles (CNP), double-walled carbon nanotubes (DWCNT) and multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWCNT) demonstrated strong model-dependent responses. Consistent with MWCNT-induced reduction in AM numbers observed in vivo, AMs GTR and BM-AMs exhibited the strongest in vitro responses, including cytotoxicity and inflammatory cytokine release. MH-S cells in contrast stood out for their cytotoxic sensitivity supporting their use for high throughput cytotoxicity tests. Overall, these findings identify AMs GTR and BM-AMs as the closest models for studying AMs biology and AM-intrinsic responses to poorly soluble nanoparticles like CBNs, and with regard to availability of higher cell numbers, BM-AMs might provide a scalable platform for mechanistic and higher-throughput nanotoxicology studies.

title: Physics-Constrained Modeling and Inference of the Equation of State for Dissociative Materials
abstract: Equations of state (EOSs) describe how a material's internal energy and pressure change with temperature and density. They are inputs to hydrodynamic simulations in materials science and planetary science. We model the ion-thermal free-energy term for dissociative materials, where molecular bonds break apart to form new species under extreme conditions. This term is governed by two latent physical processes, a molar-mass surface and a Debye-temperature curve, neither of which is observed directly. Instead, both must be recovered from internal energy and pressure, which are derivatives of the free energy, subject to thermodynamic constraints. Existing EOS tables are typically built through material-specific hand-tuning, a process that is tedious, does not scale across materials or conditions, and offers no guarantee of thermodynamic consistency. We propose a partitioned statistical framework that infers molar mass and Debye temperature directly from EOS data, guaranteeing thermodynamic consistency by construction. Local molar-mass behavior is captured with polynomial basis functions across domain partitions, while the Debye temperature is modeled with an I-spline basis. In simulations and a carbon dioxide case study, the method accurately recovers the underlying physical quantities, improves prediction of held-out energy and pressure data, and provides uncertainty quantification while scaling with EOS table size.

title: LG-Bench: A Graph-Structured Evaluation Benchmark for Life Sciences
abstract: Traditional evaluation benchmarks reduce inherently interconnected scientific knowledge in life sciences into flat lists of questions, disregarding the underlying topological structure of the knowledge. We introduce, the first graph-structured benchmark for life sciences, featuring over 10,000 high-quality multiple-choice questions across medicine, biology, and chemistry. Our approach constructs a weighted evaluation graph using bidirectional matching and semantic similarity algorithms, where nodes represent questions and edge weights capture their semantic relationships. Leveraging this graph topology, we design two novel evaluation metrics. The Global Coherence Score (GCS) measures a model's consistency within semantically related neighborhoods, while Knowledge Balance Score (KBS) analyzes how model errors are distributed across the graph to reveal conceptual blind spots. LG-Bench facilitates fine-grained comparison of LLMs by surfacing differences in conceptual coherence and patterns of knowledge organization across models. Our framework shifts the evaluation paradigm from flat accuracy metrics to structure-aware analysis, offering a new lens for diagnosing and improving LLM performance in the life sciences domain.

title: Vacuum-Field Squeezing by Molecules in Optical Cavities: An Exact Bound and Linear-Response Theory
abstract: The ground state of a molecule coupled to an optical cavity contains virtual photons, and squeezing of the photonic field has been found in exactly solvable models, perturbation theory, and numerical calculations. Here, two exact sum rules for the field quadratures show that, within the dipole approximation, the vector-potential fluctuations of a linearly polarized mode never exceed their vacuum value in the ground state of any molecule at any coupling strength. Consequently, the field is squeezed whenever the mode couples to a dipole-allowed transition from a nondegenerate ground state, and the cavity-induced ground-state energy shift cannot increase with the cavity frequency at a fixed coupling vector, which is an exact constraint on approximate methods. Moreover, the incoherent photon statistics, which exclude the coherent part of the field, are never sub-Poissonian. At weak coupling, an exact resolvent expression reduces the squeezing and the ratio of the anomalous to the normal photon moment to linear-response properties of the isolated molecule, with the ratio set by a mean excitation energy. Time-dependent density functional theory with CAM-B3LYP and PBE0 reproduces exact and QED coupled-cluster references for both quantities to within 5% at 45 benchmark points. A survey of 29 molecules gives mean excitation energies of 9.5-21 eV at a cavity frequency of 2 eV and shows that the most polarizable molecules squeeze the field the most.

title: Challenging Atomistic Foundation Models on Disordered Carbons
abstract: Foundation machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) promise broad transferability, yet their out-of-domain reliability is hard to establish. Here, we use pure and O/H-containing disordered carbon spanning multiple phases, competing hybridisations and porous frameworks to stress-test six popular foundation MLIPs. We first screen all six on density functional theory (DFT) energy and force errors and binding curves, then subject four to melt-quench-anneal molecular dynamics and evaluate the resulting structural observables. Binding curves and O/H-containing trajectories reveal unphysical extrapolation and dynamical failures that low DFT energy and force errors fail to reveal. Of the models tested, MACE-MH-1 is the most consistently robust, with low DFT errors and stable MD. Despite differing architectures, OMAT-based models share structural biases, highlighting the importance of training coverage. All four models generate structures of nanoporous carbon that reproduce the principal experimental and specialised carbon potential signatures. Incorporating O/H leaves short-range order largely unchanged but shifts pore-size distributions towards larger pores. These results emphasise the need for application-specific validation and extend molecular dynamics modelling of nanoporous carbon towards experimentally realistic structures.

title: A boundary integral method for computing electron repulsion integrals in heterogeneous dielectric environments
abstract: We present a boundary integral method for evaluating electron repulsion integrals (ERIs) in dielectric environments of piecewise constant permittivity. This generalizes conventional bare-Coulomb ERIs by incorporating screening from structured dielectric surroundings, such as the substrates and/or encapsulating layers present in modern two-dimensional-material devices. We formulate the problem as a second-kind boundary integral equation for the induced surface charge on the dielectric interfaces, and discretize it with a Nyström method on adaptively refined panels. The incident potential generated by each smooth orbital source density is evaluated by a Fourier truncated-kernel method in or near to its source box, and by fast multipole method (FMM) accelerated quadrature farther away. The linear system is solved by a Krylov iteration also accelerated by the FMM. We focus on cuboidal device geometries, and retain efficiency at high aspect ratios via close-to-touching panel quadratures. We further develop a distributed pipeline that computes the full ERI tensor, comprising thousands of orbital pairs, embedded in a single dielectric geometry. We demonstrate the method on an effective three-layer graphene slab over a Si/SiO$_2$ heterojunction, focusing on the central graphene layer represented by $198$ $p_z$-like orbitals, retaining the $2613^2$ non-negligible entries of the $198^4$-sized ERI tensor. The model is resolved on $1.3$ million surface unknowns, achieving a relative error of $0.004\%$, at a cost of $22$ node-hours.

title: recAMPLIFY: Large-Scale Pretraining of Recursive Protein Language Models
abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) are powerful tools for protein annotation and mutation-effect prediction, but progress has largely depended on scaling model size and data, making them expensive and prone to memorization. Test-time scaling offers a complementary path, but methods developed for autoregressive LLMs do not transfer directly: masked encoders lack a generation loop, and amino acids do not verbalize in a reasoning language. Instead, we adapt recursive pretraining to masked pLMs, where a weight-tied Transformer core refines residue-aligned hidden states over an adjustable number of cycles. We instantiate this recipe as recAMPLIFY, a pLM with 155M unique parameters trained on the same 2T tokens as AMPLIFY-350M. Despite 56% fewer parameters, it improves CASP contact recovery and three out of four supervised tasks, notably raising fold accuracy by 22.5%. Because optimal depth for recAMPLIFY varies across tasks and assays, we then introduce Gated Mixture Recurrence (GMR), a framework that decodes each protein from a probability-weighted mixture of hidden states visited during recursion. GMR employs a learned residual gate at scalar, low-rank, or per-dimension resolution to control how much of each cycle's proposed update is accepted into the state. This unifies halting and gating into a single adaptive computation objective while recovering PonderNet-style halting as a special case without gates. Layered on top of recAMPLIFY, GMR further reduces expected layer depth by up to 37%, although the accuracy trade-off varies by task. Mechanistic analyses show that residual gating controls recurrence stability beyond the trained depth and that halt depth tracks biological properties.

title: 1,3- cis -Disubstituted Cycloalkanes by Iridium-Catalyzed Enantio-convergent Migratory Hydroheteroarylation
abstract: Enantioenriched 1,3-disubstituted cycloalkanes are important structural motifs in pharmaceuticals and natural products, yet their stereoselective synthesis remains challenging owing to difficulties in remote control of regio- and stereoselectivities. Herein, we report an iridium-catalyzed enantio-convergent hydroheteroarylation of racemic unactivated cyclic alkenes through a dynamic kinetic asymmetric transformation (DYKAT).
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Frozen in action: Visualizing how a cancer drug scaffold is built
abstract: A joint research group led by Ryo Tanifuji and Hiroki Oguri from the University of Tokyo and Yoshikazu Tanaka from Tohoku University has visualized SacC, an enzyme that plays a key role in building the complex five-ring core of safracin B. This core structure is shared with trabectedin, a drug used to treat soft tissue sarcoma.

title: A qualitative and quantitative framework for the characterization of protein-RNA interactions by cross-linking mass spectrometry (XL-MS)
abstract: Protein-RNA interactions regulate nearly all levels of gene expression. Their characterization at the molecular basis is critical for understanding the function of protein-RNA complexes, both in cell homeostasis and pathology. Yet, molecular interactions underlying the formation of these complexes remain understudied. UV cross-linking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) is one of the leading approaches for in vitro identification of protein-RNA contact sites, and for providing structural information in the form of distance constraints crucial for the refinement of structural models. Our previously published CLIR-MS method enables qualitative characterization of protein-RNA interactions at residue-specific resolution but was not designed for highly accurate quantitative interpretation. Here, we present a XL-MS workflow based on irradiation with UV light that combines data-dependent acquisition (DDA) and parallel reaction monitoring (PRM) for simultaneous detection and characterization of protein-RNA interaction sites at residue-specific resolution, followed by label-free quantification of cross-linked products. We successfully apply our combined workflow to in vitro reconstituted protein-RNA complexes formed by the proteins TDP-43 and FOX1. We report on novel RNA interaction sites located in the oligomerization interface of the N-terminal domain (NTD) of TDP-43, and characterize quantitatively the process of RNA-induced monomerization of the NTD in an RNA titration experiment. We also investigate temperature-dependent differences in the efficiency of cross-link formation in the FOX1 complex. Our framework offers a unique and novel approach to comparative quantification of protein-RNA cross-links, overcoming the limitations imposed by conventional UV XL-MS methods.

title: Safe Reinforcement Learning for Energy Management of EV-Integrated Renewable Microgrids in Sub-Saharan Africa: A Methodology Proposal
abstract: Energy management in solar-based microgrids that also serve electric vehicles (EVs) in sub-Saharan Africa must cope with scarce measurement data, unreliable grid supply, volatile demand and tight battery and generator limits. Reinforcement learning (RL) can adapt to this uncertainty, but unconstrained RL policies give no assurance that operating limits are respected, and most published methods are validated on data-rich systems outside the region.

title: Planar Benzene Trianion-Bridged Dilanthanide Complexes Exhibiting Strong Ferromagnetic Exchange via Metal–Radical Covalency
abstract: The synthesis of molecules exhibiting strong magnetic exchange coupling between contracted lanthanide 4f electrons and a radical spin presents an important challenge relevant to the design of single-molecule magnets and solid-state magnetic materials. Concurrently, the isolation of a planar benzene trianion radical remains an unrealized target. Here, we report the synthesis and characterization of the dilanthanide compounds [(CpiPr5Ln)2(μ-η6:η6-C6H6)][Fe(N(SiMe3)2)3] (Ln = Y, Gd, Tb, Dy, Ho, Er, Tm; CpiPr5 = pentaisopropylcyclopentadienyl), featuring cationic inverse sandwich complexes in…
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: A Critical Spin Moment Governs the Spin-Adsorption Relationship in Magnetic Single-Atom Alloys
abstract: Spin engineering has emerged as a promising strategy for tuning catalytic activity by manipulating the spin states of active sites. This strategy generally assumes that the local spin moment serves as a universal descriptor for adsorption strength, yet its validity remains largely unexplored. Here, we develop a reverse doping strategy that enables broad modulation of local spin moments in magnetic single-atom alloy catalysts, allowing the spin–adsorption relationship to be systematically revisited.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Residual-Based Adaptive Refinement in Hybrid Variational-Collocation PINNs for Singular Elliptic PDEs with Mixed Dirichlet-Neumann Boundary Conditions
abstract: Solutions of second-order elliptic PDE problems on nonconvex or cracked domains with mixed Dirichlet-Neumann conditions typically lie outside $H^2(Ω)$. Near re-entrant corners, crack tips and points where the boundary condition changes type, the gradient grows like $r^{λ-1}$ with $λ<1$. We study residual-based adaptive refinement in hybrid variational-collocation PINNs. A multiscale Fourier-feature network is trained on a composite loss. The loss combines a variational residual tested against Legendre bubble functions, a strong-form collocation term and penalties for the Dirichlet and Neumann data. The variational term needs only first derivatives of the network, whereas the collocation term requires second derivatives and provides a residual that can be evaluated at any point. After each training stage, candidate points selected by this residual are added to the collocation set. The method is tested on five two dimensional benchmarks, namely a Mode~III crack, a cross-shaped domain with four re-entrant corners with unequal amplitude, a reaction-diffusion problem with four localized peaks, a monotone semilinear problem with a boundary layer and the Motz problem. Compared with uniform point insertion under the same collocation and iteration budget, residual-based refinement reduced the relative $L^2$ error by up to a factor of $32$, the relative $L^\infty$ error by up to a factor of $38$ and the relative $H^1$ semi-norm error by up to a factor of $15$.

title: Composable, Knowledge-Driven Disservice Propagation for Complex Interdependent Services with a Flow-Allocation Module Validated Against Hydraulic Simulation
abstract: Modeling cascading failure across interdependent critical infrastructure requires either a composable physical simulator per domain or a topological abstraction that discards quantity awareness. Simulators are costly, data-hungry, and require detailed calibration per domain; topological abstractions stay data-parsimonious while missing quantity-based behaviors that govern real dynamics. We present, instead, a knowledge-driven propagation architecture in which heterogeneous service dependencies are identified by categories: a general logical propagation resolves multi-dependency and redundancy structures purely from how nodes are categorized, while quantity-aware categories plug in dedicated mechanisms - here, a max-min fair-share flow module for water distribution. Both share one discrete functionality scale and a monotonic update algorithm guaranteeing convergence in finitely many rounds. We assess the flow module by comparing its results with those we get from preexisting pressure-driven simulation with WNTR (Water Network Tool for Resilience) on eight realistic networks across four failure families (clustered damage, capacity-targeted attack, source failure, tank loss). Under capacity-targeted attack and source failure a topological-reachability baseline misses 46% of the truly critical junctions, where the flow module misses 10% and 8% at an average critical-class precision of 0.73. Supplementary materials, code and results are available at: https://github.com/cascade-platform-org/CASCADE

title: Coupling Evaporation, Chemical Reactions, and Crystallization: A Population-Balance Framework Applied to Two-Step Perovskite Crystallization
abstract: A limited understanding of how evaporation couples to crystallization pathways hampers control over the formation of solution-processed perovskite photoactive layers. Identifying these mechanisms-and learning how to select and tune them-is essential for achieving the desired crystal morphology and, ultimately, improving solar-cell performance and stability. To investigate crystallization pathways in evaporating thin films, we develop a simple and general zero-dimensional population-balance model that couples evaporation, chemical reactions, and crystallization. We use the model to explore a range of parameters for a solvent-solute system that follows a two-step crystallization pathway: solvent evaporation first induces formation of a crystalline precursor, which subsequently recrystallizes into the final phase. The model predicts the evolution of the film composition during drying and provides quantitative LaMer curves. Based on these results, we introduce a vocabulary of "supply limitations" and "rate limitations" that enables the interpretation of crystallization kinetics in terms of the governing process conditions.

title: Localized and Delocalized Nonadiabatic Vibronic Models Unravel Chiroptical Trends and Design Principles in Symmetric π Conjugated Macrocycles
abstract: The chiroptical response of π-conjugated macrocycles assembled from repeating chromophores can be remarkably intense, yet how it scales with ring size, and what controls it, remains only partly understood. Here we investigate a series of axially chiral diethynylspirobifluorene macrocycles, (Pn)-DESn (n = 2, 3, 4; D2, D3 and D4 symmetry), combining accurate nonadiabatic quantum dynamics with two complementary linear vibronic coupling Hamiltonians: a delocalized model, whose diabatic states span the whole macrocycle, and a localized, exciton-like model built from the excitations of the individual fragments. Both reproduce the experimental one-photon absorption and electronic circular dichroism (ECD) spectra and reveal that nonadiabatic interactions, conical intersections and (pseudo-)Jahn–Teller couplings govern their shapes; a hierarchical representation of the Hamiltonian keeps the simulations tractable, even for (P4)-DES4, with more than 500 vibrational modes. A simple symmetry analysis bridges the two pictures, tracing every coupling back to the single excited-state gradient of the monomer and partitions the magnetic transition dipole into an intrinsic contribution, from the strained monomer and an extrinsic, excitonic one. This decomposition rationalizes the observed trends explaining why the ECD grows super-linearly with ring size. As a result, the response crosses over from strain-dominated chirality in (P2)-DES2 to excitonic chirality in (P4)-DES4 at a nearly constant dissymmetry factor. Crucially, the excitonic rotatory strengths form a nearly conservative couplet whose oppositely signed branches partly cancel, and their splitting (0.12–0.16 eV) is comparable to the width of the vibronic progressions. The intrinsic band shape of the monomer, not the splitting alone, therefore sets how much ECD survives. We translate these findings into geometric, excitonic and vibronic design principles for g-factor improved symmetric chiral macrocycles, suggesting that our proposed computational approach can be a fast screening tool for new designed macrocycles before synthesis.
venue: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

title: Inferring protein-induced spontaneous curvature of lipid bilayers from molecular simulation
abstract: Proteins and lipids of a biological cell work together to reshape the membranes in which they reside. Membrane reshaping is necessary for vesicular traffic and maintenance of organelle shape and structure. Curvature is the fundamental mathematical description of the local shape of a surface. Through the well-established Helfrich/Canham/Evans model of bilayer shape, curvature sensing and induction are both consequences of a protein's spontaneous curvature, the local curvature at which the Helfrich model energy is a minimum. This paper describes a straightforward approach for estimating the strength and sign of a bilayer-associated molecule's curvature induction from molecular simulation: Correlating the molecule's lateral position with curvature on thermally-fluctuating bilayer modes. Example demonstrations range from a large multi-pass coarse-grained transmembrane protein to an all-atom amphipathic helical segment. Quantification of these systems is placed in the context of experiments seeking the same strength and sign of curvature induction.

title: Structural order emerges without mechanical order inside living cells
abstract: Intracellular organization is vital for cell function, and disruption of organelle positioning is connected to severe diseases, such as cancer. Given the small length scale of cells and the importance of Brownian motion, maintaining intracellular organization requires mechanical interactions to remain stable. Here, we test the common view that intracellular organization is reflected in intracellular mechanical properties. Using the recently introduced active mechanical fingerprint, we quantify intracellular mechanical properties and active forces to create mechanical maps of patterned RPE1 cells. The organization of actin, microtubules, the Golgi apparatus, the endoplasmic reticulum, and the nucleus reveals pronounced structural polarization across the cell population. To overcome limitations of simple averages, we use a Wasserstein barycenter to calculate an optimal intracellular organization that explains all measurements with minimal cellular distortion. To our surprise, and in contrast to previous reports, we find neither a statistically significant spatial mechanical pattern nor any relevant correlation between the tested structures and intracellular mechanical properties. While there is clear local mechanical anisotropy, the large heterogeneity of mechanical values outweighs any intracellular mechanical gradient. This is further supported by large cell-to-cell variability. Thus, despite having the same genome, cells function properly while their intracellular mechanical properties vary over two orders of magnitude.

title: Fluorescent Biosensors for Cryogenic Correlative Light and Electron Microscopy
abstract: Cryogenic electron tomography provides nanometer-scale views of subcellular structures but lacks essential physiological context, such as the metabolic state or ion concentration. To bridge this gap, we incorporated fluorescent biosensors into a cryogenic correlative light and electron microscopy workflow, enabling direct measurement of physiological conditions alongside structural data. Here, we focused on establishing and calibrating biosensors for calcium, pH, and osmotic stress at cryogenic conditions through an in vitro workflow in which biosensors were frozen in defined chemical environments and then imaged ratiometrically. We then applied these biosensors across a range of sample types: an osmotic stress sensor in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, a calcium sensor in human U2OS cells, and a pH sensor in the bacterium Halothiobacillus neapolitanus. This approach links localized physiological changes to the 3D structures of macromolecules and their organization in situ.

title: CiliaBuilder2: a flexible ChimeraX bundle to visualize cilia and centriole structures in 3D
abstract: Centrioles and cilia are large organelles essential for cell division, motility, and signalling. They are characterized by distinctive, nine-fold symmetric microtubule doublets or triplets decorated with periodic protein complexes. While cilia and centrioles are highly conserved across eukaryotes, their composition and structure vary considerably between species and tissue types. Advances in cryo-electron tomography and single-particle cryo-electron microscopy have recently led to a surge in structural data for ciliary components. However, visualizing these components within the ciliary context remains challenging due to their scale and the diverse data formats involved, such as density maps, atomic models, and 3D geometric objects. Here, we introduce CiliaBuilder2, a toolset integrated into UCSF ChimeraX that enables simple, flexible visualization of complete ciliary structures from diverse data types using parametric calculations.

title: Direct Amidination of Alkenes Via C–H Activation of Pyridinyl Formimidamide Synthon
abstract: Alkenes are among the most abundant and versatile feedstocks in synthetic chemistry, yet methods for their direct and regioselective conversion into nitrogen-containing frameworks remain scarce. In particular, the direct catalytic amidination of alkenes has remained underdeveloped. Herein, we report a rhodium-catalyzed anti-Markovnikov amidination of alkenes using a stable pyridinyl formimidamide synthon.

title: Combining transcriptomics, single-cell data, and a combination of 113-combination machine learning framework, as well as experimental verification, identified the key genes related to lactylation modifications in ulcerative colitis
abstract: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease characterized by immune dysregulation and mucosal inflammation. This study aims to elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying UC by identifying key genetic markers and potential therapeutic targets.The GSE75214 dataset was used for differential expression analysis, and candidate genes were identified through cross-validation with known lactylation-related genes (LRGs).

title: REFLEX: RNA Ensemble Generation via Flexibility-Calibrated Stochastic Bridge
abstract: RNA molecules often function through multiple experimentally observed conformational states. A central challenge is to capture ensemble diversity without sacrificing structural fidelity: samples may collapse toward averaged representative structures or drift into unsupported conformational regions. We introduce REFLEX (RNA Ensemble generation calibrated by FLEXibility), a sequence-conditioned generator for RNA backbone-frame ensembles based on a heteroscedastic stochastic bridge on SE(3). During training, experimental B-factors calibrate residue-wise bridge widths, exposing each observed conformer through local perturbation neighborhoods with residue-specific scales while keeping constrained regions sharper. A learned flexibility condition guides the bridge-field network to recover target conformer-specific frames from these calibrated noisy states. At inference, REFLEX uses only the input sequence, requiring no MSA-subsampling heuristics. On a multi-conformer RNA benchmark, REFLEX achieves the best precision-recall trade-off for ensemble coverage across evaluation thresholds, while recovery-stress ablations indicate gains in target-frame recovery under stronger perturbations.

title: Sidewall Metrology Protocol for Superconducting Qubit Devices
abstract: Sidewall morphology is a potentially important factor influencing superconducting qubit performance, yet its quantitative characterization remains challenging due to the absence of standardized measurement protocols. In this work, we develop a scanning probe microscopy-based measurement framework for the quantitative characterization of superconducting qubit sidewalls. The framework introduces a refined root mean square lateral sidewall roughness descriptor and a new curvature-equivalent radius for quantifying vertical sidewall morphology. The descriptors and measurement procedures are applied to different components of qubit devices, forming the basis of a proposed sidewall characterization protocol. This provides a foundation for quantitative comparisons of fabrication processes across laboratories, enabling future investigations of correlations between sidewall geometry and qubit performance.

title: Hidden piezo-Hall effect
abstract: Extensive studies of hidden spin polarization have established a broad class of hidden phenomena in quantum materials. Here, we introduce the hidden piezo-Hall effect, in which strain induces finite anomalous Hall conductivities (AHCs) in individual sectors while the global AHC remains zero. At zero strain, neither the full system nor its sectors exhibit an anomalous Hall effect (AHE). Under uniaxial strain, however, opposite sector AHCs emerge while their sum remains canceled. We establish this effect for a $d$-wave hidden altermagnet using a tight-binding model and first-principles calculations for the experimentally synthesized material $\mathrm{RbV_2Te_2O}$. Rotating the strain direction from the $x$ to the $y$ axis reverses the signs of the sector AHCs without generating a net Hall response. The same symmetry mechanism may also give rise to hidden piezomagneto-optical, piezo-thermal Hall, piezo-Nernst, and piezo-Ettingshausen effects. Our work extends hidden physics to strain-controlled transport and identifies $\mathrm{RbV_2Te_2O}$ as a promising candidate for experimental verification.

title: Proximate, Mineral and Anti-nutrient Composition of Fermented Cassava Product (Pupuru) Supplemented with Fermented Moringa oleifera Seed.
abstract: Background: Pupuru, a traditionally fermented and smoked-dried cassava (Manihot esculenta) product, is widely consumed in South-Western Nigeria but is limited by low protein content and poor nutritional profile. Objective: This study investigated the proximate composition, mineral profiles, and anti-nutritional factors of Pupuru supplemented with fermented Moringa oleifera seeds at varying inclusion levels. Methods: Fermented cassava mash was supplemented with fermented Moringa oleifera seeds at 0% (control), 1%, 5%, and 10% inclusion levels. The resulting flour blends were analyzed for proximate composition, macro- and micromineral content, and anti-nutritional factors using standard AOAC methods. Results: Supplementation significantly (p<0.05) increased protein (1.43-4.33%), fat (0.28-0.87%), fiber (0.32-0.75%), ash (0.40-1.30%), and moisture (12.57-13.06%) contents while carbohydrate content decreased (84.52-80.20%). Mineral profiles improved significantly across all treatment levels for iron (18.28-22.40 mg/kg), zinc (7.71-12.51 mg/kg), manganese (3.66-8.91 mg/kg), and copper (0.67-1.14 mg/kg). Anti-nutritional factors including phytate (0.27-0.30%), saponin (0.05-0.09%), oxalate (0.13-0.16%), and tannin remained within acceptable limits. Conclusion: Moringa oleifera seed supplementation significantly improved the nutritional quality of Pupuru without compromising its safety profile, presenting a viable strategy for addressing protein-calorie malnutrition and mineral deficiencies in cassava-consuming populations.

title: Towards VDAC pharmacology: Developing small-peptide channel inhibitors inspired by nature
abstract: The Voltage-Dependent Anion Channel (VDAC) forms a unique pathway across the mitochondrial outer membrane for small ions and water-soluble metabolites, such as ATP and ADP. Despite VDAC's involvement in both normal regulation of respiration and in a wide variety of mitochondria-associated pathologies, there are, surprisingly, no known FDA-approved pharmacological agents targeting VDAC. Earlier, we have shown that VDAC can be regulated through its interactions with well-known cytosolic proteins--dimeric tubulin and -synuclein (Syn)--that are able to reversibly block this channel at nanomolar concentrations. We hypothesized that the architecture of a prospective VDAC inhibitor should fulfill two main requirements: possess a negatively charged disordered polypeptide C- or N-terminus as a pore blocking domain and feature a mitochondrial membrane-binding domain. Using Syn as a template, we engineered three peptides and demonstrated that they all characteristically block VDAC reconstituted into planar lipid membranes in a controllable manner, thereby mimicking the actions of tubulin and Syn. The VDAC blockage times induced by the synthetic peptides are comparable to Syn-induced blockages, though the half-effect solution concentration for synthetic blockers is a hundred times higher than that of Syn. Our work can be considered a proof-of-principle study that informs future development of mitochondria-targeting pharmacological tools.

title: So similar, yet so different: α-synuclein recognition of the isoform-specific VDAC protein-lipid interface
abstract: In mammals, VDAC exists as three isoforms--VDAC1, VDAC2, and VDAC3--each characterized by a distinct tissue-dependent distribution and physiologic role. Isoform-specific knockout studies in cells and mice demonstrate distinct physiological roles for each VDAC isoform. The isoforms share about 70% sequence homology and a conserved {beta}-barrel structure and, when reconstituted into planar lipid membranes, form similar highly conductive, anion-selective, voltage-gated channels. A natural question, then, is how relatively minor differences in isoform sequences lead to striking differences in their interactions with protein partners and, consequently, in their physiological functions. To address this question, we used a small, intrinsically disordered cytosolic protein -synuclein (Syn) as a sensitive molecular probe. A comparative study with recombinant VDACs reconstituted into planar lipid membranes shows that, depending on the isoform, the Syn-induced blockage exhibits up to 100-fold differences in on-rates and equilibrium constants. The isoforms also display distinct translocation regimes for Syn, as evidenced by altered dependences of the off-rates on the applied voltage. Deletion of cysteine residues has a significant effect on Syn binding. Combined with corresponding data obtained for VDAC2 substates--which show an order of magnitude variation in on-rates while maintaining the conserved equilibrium constants--and the results of molecular dynamics simulations, these findings point to a previously unrecognized step in VDAC inhibition by Syn: an isoform-specific Syn interaction with the VDAC protein-lipid interface. This finding opens a new paradigm for understanding VDAC isoform functions and developing isoform-specific therapeutics.

title: Extremophilic Laccase-Mediator System Enabling Near-Complete Degradation of Doxycycline.
abstract: Using an extremophilic laccase with a phenolic redox mediator, we rapidly abolished doxycycline antibacterial activity and achieved near-complete chemical degradation (>97%) within 2 h under mild conditions. Antibiotic residues in aquatic and terrestrial environments drive the emergence and spread of microbial resistance genes, yet many treatment strategies are limited by slow kinetics or incomplete transformation. Here, we evaluated doxycycline degradation by the recombinant FNT laccase across pH and temperature conditions, comparing direct enzymatic oxidation with a laccase-mediator system. RP-HPLC quantified doxycycline removal. Residual toxicity was assessed using growth inhibition assays with Bacillus subtilis and Escherichia coli BL21. In the absence of a mediator, oxidation produced only partial loss of function, indicating that structural modification alone does not guarantee pharmacological inactivation. In contrast, the addition of acetosyringone markedly increased biodegradation efficiency, yielding >97% doxycycline depletion and eliminating antibacterial activity. To rationalize condition-dependent performance, we complemented experiments with molecular simulations of doxycycline binding at the laccase active site, revealing pH-dependent differences in stability and substrate interactions consistent with enhanced turnover under alkaline conditions. These results demonstrate that an extremophilic laccase-mediator system provides rapid, effective detoxification of doxycycline, supporting its potential for treatment of antibiotic-contaminated effluents.

title: Counterexamples to the total-current Hohenberg-Kohn conjecture
abstract: The total-current Hohenberg-Kohn conjecture asserts that the ground-state particle density and total current determine the scalar potential up to an additive constant and the vector potential up to a gauge transformation. We give three counterexamples for two spinless fermions in the physically relevant setting of three spatial dimensions. In each, a Hamiltonian $H^{v,\mathbf{A}}$ has a nondegenerate ground state with identically zero total current but nonzero magnetic field. Complex conjugation then yields a second Hamiltonian $H^{v,-\mathbf{A}}$, with the same scalar potential and interaction, whose ground state has the same density and the same zero current, while the magnetic field is reversed. The first two examples are noninteracting. One is explicit, with a smooth bounded vector potential and a Gaussian density. The other has smooth bounded scalar and vector potentials in the standard potential spaces. The third example has Coulomb repulsion with unit coupling, an isotropic harmonic scalar potential, and Dirac monopole fields of magnetic charge $\pm 1/2$. The monopole example uses vector potentials defined on separate spatial patches, since these fields are not curls of globally defined smooth vector potentials.

title: Surprisingly high redundancy in electronic structure data across materials explained by low intrinsic dimensionality
abstract: Machine learning (ML) models for electronic structure typically rely on large datasets generated by computationally expensive Kohn-Sham density functional theory calculations, as it is not known a priori which portions of the data are essential for accurate learning. Here, we reveal significant redundancies in electronic structure datasets across diverse material systems and attribute them to the low intrinsic dimensionality of the underlying data. We show that even random pruning can substantially reduce dataset size with minimal degradation in predictive accuracy. Moreover, a state-of-the-art coverage-based pruning strategy that samples data across all learning difficulties almost always preserves chemical accuracy and maintains model generalizability while using up to two orders of magnitude less data and reducing training time by a factor of three or more. We further demonstrate that the essential electronic structure information lies on a low-dimensional, non-linear manifold, providing a potential geometric explanation for the observed prunability. These observations are consistent with the predominance of local atomic environments in determining electronic properties, as suggested by nearsightedness arguments, and indicate that large-scale datasets may contain highly overlapping information. Our findings challenge the prevailing assumption that such extensive datasets are necessary for accurate ML-based electronic structure predictions and open a path toward identifying minimal, representative datasets for each material class.
